messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error (standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}
\]

\[
\sqrt{40}\approx 6.3249 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; SE \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249}\approx 0.221
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis sampling distribution (the standard error of the mean) is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning: The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely means the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. Standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they might want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null. That is indeed the standard error. So compute 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ~ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So about 0.221. Alternatively, if they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic? Usually we compute the standard error of the mean. So answer: approximately 0.221. Provide explanation.
